headline: Kowai is a semantic shift from classical 強し (kofashi, “stiff, strong, tough”), and one folk etymology reads it as 狐者異.
Matsu is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mat-, with an Okinawan cognate.
Kaeru is cognate with 返る (kaeru, “to return”), by extension of returning to one's home.
Fukai was fukashi in Early Middle Japanese, before its ending was replaced and the medial k fell out.
Kieru is from the classical lower bigrade verb 消ゆ.
Gogo is a compound of 午 (go, “noon”) plus 後 (go, “after-, post-”).
Kirai is the stem form of the verb 嫌う (kirau, “to detest, dislike, hate”).
Aoi was Old Japanese awosi, from awo-, from Proto-Japonic *awo.
Man is from Middle Chinese 萬 (MC mjonH).
Haisha is 歯 (ha, “tooth”) plus 医者 (isha, “doctor”).
Shiai is し (shi, the stem of する) plus 合い (ai, the stem of 合う).
Naku is 音 (na, “(emotional) sound, voice”) plus く (-ku, verb suffix), cognate with 鳴く (naku).
Yokka is considered a shift from 四日 (yoka), a compound of 四 (yo, “four”) plus 日 (-ka, counter for days).
Hako was pako, and originally referred to a kind of wicker basket or box introduced from continental Asia.
Otto was wofito, a compound of 男 (wo, “male, man”) plus 人 (fito, “person”), first attested in roughly 1220.
Okurimono is 贈る (okuru) plus 物 (-mono).
Kokoro is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *kəkərə.
Abiru comes from the classical upper bigrade verb 浴ぶ, possibly from 浴む (amu).
Haizara is 灰 (hai, “ash”) plus 皿 (sara, “plate”), and sara changes to zara by rendaku.
Karui was seldom used outside of proper nouns in Old Japanese, spelled 軽 in the Man'yōshū.
Iu was ipu: the p became an f sound, then w, and a w before u never surfaced.
Midori originally referred to new buds and shoots, later expanding via metonymy to mean green.
Uchi is a doublet of 家 (uchi), from Proto-Japonic *utui.
Roku is from Middle Chinese 六 (MC ljuwk).
Mae is a compound of 目 (ma, “eye”) plus 方 (pe1, “direction, -wards”) in Old Japanese.
Chiisana appears starting from the Muromachi period, as the -na adjective form of 小さい.
Yoko is from Proto-Japonic *yəkə, with cognates in Kunigami, Miyako, Okinawan and Yaeyama.
Toshokan is 図書 (tosho, “books”) plus 館 (-kan, “building”).
Tsutomeru is a doublet of 務める (tsutomeru).
Okusan is equivalent to 奥 (oku) plus さん (san), from 奥様 (okusama).
Niwa went /nipa/ → /nifa/ → /niwa/ from Old Japanese.
